body: Which of the following is the correct order Mr Songo must follow in assessing his Basic 5 pupils?

options.hint: Correct. Administer the test, score (measure) it, then judge (evaluate).

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **test** is the instrument; **measurement** assigns numbers (scores) to performance; **evaluation** makes a value judgement using those scores. So: test → measure → evaluate.

## Simplified explanation

Test, then score, then judge.

body: To identify each college during an inter-college quiz competition (e.g. College A, B, C), which scale of measurement will the organisers use?

options.hint: That ranks; here there's no order.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Nominal** scales use numbers or labels purely to **identify or classify** (jersey numbers, college codes). **Ordinal** ranks; **interval** has equal units but no true zero; **ratio** has a true zero.

## Simplified explanation

Labels that only identify = **nominal**.

body: Which characteristic allows **ratio** scores to be multiplied and divided?

options.hint: Correct. Zero means none of the attribute.
Interval scales have these but can't be multiplied meaningfully.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Only a **ratio** scale has a **true zero**, so statements like 'twice as much' make sense (e.g. 20 pupils is twice 10 pupils).

## Simplified explanation

A **true zero**.

body: **True or False?** Equal intervals in the interval scale make it possible for scores to be multiplied and divided.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Interval scales (e.g. °C) have equal units but an **arbitrary zero**, so you can add/subtract but not form meaningful ratios (40 °C is not 'twice as hot' as 20 °C).

## Simplified explanation

Needs a true zero, so false.

body: A teacher measures many variables in his school. An example of a variable measured on a **ratio** scale is the

options.hint: Correct. Counts have a true zero.

options.text: singing ability of the school choir

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Counts such as **enrolment** start from a true zero and can be compared as ratios.

## Simplified explanation

Counts → ratio.

body: Mary spends a lot of time learning but still fails her exams. Which type of assessment will help her to understand herself as a learner, adopt proper learning methods and plan her future learning?

options.hint: Correct. Self-assessment and reflection by the learner.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**AaL** puts the learner at the centre: she monitors her own learning (metacognition) and adjusts strategies. **AfL** is teacher feedback to improve learning; **AoL** certifies achievement.

## Simplified explanation

Self-reflection = **assessment as learning**.

body: Which level of the **affective** domain requires the student to relate what has been learnt to their existing values (schema) in order to accommodate it?

options.hint: A value system that controls behaviour.
Correct. Bringing values together and resolving conflicts between them.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Krathwohl's affective domain: **receiving → responding → valuing → organisation → characterisation (by a value complex)**. **Organisation** integrates new values into one's value system.

## Simplified explanation

Fitting new values into your system = **organisation**.

body: Which level of the **cognitive** domain represents students' ability to identify and establish the relationships among the component parts of a product?

options.hint: Putting parts together into a new whole.
Correct. Breaking a whole into parts and seeing how they relate.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bloom: **analysis** = breaking material into its parts and examining their relationships.

## Simplified explanation

Parts and relationships = **analysis**.

body: The illustrative verb **'outline'** represents which dimension of the cognitive taxonomy?

options.hint: Correct. Summarising the main points in one's own way.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Outlining (summarising main points) shows **comprehension/understanding**. Knowledge = recall; analysis = break down; synthesis = create.

## Simplified explanation

**Understanding**.

body: A teacher's remarks such as 'proficient', 'beginner', 'advanced' represent

options.hint: The broader process of gathering information.
Correct. Judgements about the quality of performance.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Descriptors of quality are **value judgements**: that is **evaluation**.

## Simplified explanation

Judging quality = **evaluation**.

body: In Bloom's Taxonomy (cognitive domain), 'analysis and synthesis' are considered more fundamental (they appear earlier in the taxonomy) than

options.hint: Correct. Evaluation is the highest level in the original taxonomy.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Original Bloom order: **knowledge → comprehension → application → analysis → synthesis → evaluation**.

## Simplified explanation

Only **evaluation** comes after them.

body: Which of the following is a category in the taxonomy of educational objectives of the **affective** domain?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Affective levels: receiving, responding, **valuing**, organisation, characterisation.

## Simplified explanation

**Valuing**.

body: The type of assessment that does **not** expect mastery when students are introduced to new concepts is

options.hint: Who conducts it, not its purpose.
Correct. It monitors progress during learning.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Formative** assessment happens during learning to guide teaching; students are still developing mastery.

## Simplified explanation

During learning = **formative**.

body: A general instructional objective that produces outcomes focused on **perceptual processes and motor skills** belongs to the

options.hint: A way of stating objectives, not a domain.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **psychomotor** domain covers perception, movement and manipulative skills.

## Simplified explanation

Motor skills = **psychomotor**.

body: A purposeful, systematic and ongoing collection of information as evidence for making judgements about students' learning, curricula, programmes and policies is
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Assessment** is the broad, ongoing process of collecting evidence; evaluation is the judgement made from it.

## Simplified explanation

**Assessment**.

body: Judgements about the worth of schools, curricula, materials and programmes **while they are under development**, leading to suggestions for redesign or improvement, are
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Formative** evaluation improves a programme while it is being developed; **summative** evaluation judges its overall effectiveness at the end.

## Simplified explanation

During development = **formative**.

body: Which of the following scores can vary across assessments of the same individual?

options.text: Both the error score and the observed score
options.hint: Correct. Only the true score is constant.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Classical test theory: **observed = true + error**. The true score is fixed; random error changes from one testing to another, so observed scores vary too.

## Simplified explanation

True score fixed; error and observed vary.

body: The standard error of measurement (SEM) of a test is 4. A student obtained 76. How should the score be interpreted? The student's

options.text: obtained score would be between 72 and 76
true score would be increased to 80
error score would be raised to 19

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A band of **observed score ± SEM** (76 ± 4 = 72–80) contains the true score about 68% of the time (± 2 SEM ≈ 95%).

## Simplified explanation

76 ± 4 → **72–80**.

body: If assessment results measure a sample of behaviour **consistently** but lack soundness of interpretation and use, the test is

options.hint: Correct. Consistent but not measuring what it should.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Reliability** = consistency; **validity** = soundness of interpretation and use. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

## Simplified explanation

Consistent but wrong use = **reliable, not valid**.

body: A characteristic of **assessment of learning (AoL)** is that it is

options.text: conducted at the end of a unit
used to give feedback during instruction
used to describe needs for future learning
conducted during a unit of instruction

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

AoL is **summative**: it certifies or grades achievement at the end of a unit, term or course.

## Simplified explanation

AoL = end of unit.

body: The **test–retest** method of estimating reliability is a measure of the

options.text: stability of test scores over time

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Test–retest gives a **coefficient of stability**; equivalent forms gives **equivalence**; split-half/KR-20/alpha give **internal consistency**; inter-rater gives scorer agreement.

## Simplified explanation

Two occasions → **stability**.

body: Consider: I. Validity is impossible without strong reliability. II. A test can be reliable without being valid. III. A valid test is reliable. Which statement(s) is/are correct?

options.hint: Correct. All three express the reliability–validity relationship.
II and III are also true.
I and II are also true.
I and III are also true.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reliability is a **necessary but not sufficient** condition for validity: a valid test must be reliable (I, III), but a reliable test need not be valid (II).

## Simplified explanation

All three are true.

body: Mr Hutton asks the other maths teachers to review his mid-term test to see if the items represent his learning targets. Which type of validity evidence is being used?

options.hint: Does it measure the theoretical trait?
Correct. Do the items represent the content/targets?

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Content validity** is judged by experts comparing items with the table of specifications/learning targets.

## Simplified explanation

Experts check coverage = **content validity**.

body: Which method of estimating reliability is most useful for determining how far essay scores from different raters are affected by differences in the raters' strictness?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Inter-rater (scorer) reliability** compares scores given independently by different markers.

## Simplified explanation

Different markers → **inter-rater**.

body: The learning target 'the student contributes to group maintenance when working with classmates on a science project' belongs to the
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cooperation and willingness to support a group are **attitudes/values**: the affective domain.

## Simplified explanation

Group attitudes = **affective**.

body: 'Araba is able to adjust a 70-inch LED television set to get the best picture and colour resolution.' This learning target belongs to the
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Operating and adjusting equipment is a **manipulative (psychomotor)** skill.

## Simplified explanation

Hands-on skill = **psychomotor**.

body: 'Obedii virtually displaced the goalkeeper and scored through a free kick awarded 35 m from the post.' This learning target belongs to the
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Skilled movement and coordination = **psychomotor**.

## Simplified explanation

**Psychomotor**.

body: Explain briefly the **'comprehensive'** characteristic of assessment.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Assessment is **comprehensive** when it covers **all aspects of the learner's development**, cognitive, affective and psychomotor, and the full range of learning outcomes, using a **variety of methods** (tests, projects, observation, portfolios, oral work) over time, rather than relying on a single test of knowledge.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Comprehensive assessment gives a fuller, fairer picture of what a learner knows and can do.

## Simplified explanation

Assess the whole learner with many methods.

body: (a) State **four** methods of estimating reliability, and explain any two with examples. (b) Describe **five** factors that influence the reliability of test scores.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a) Methods:**
> 1. **Test–retest**: give the same test twice to the same group after an interval; correlate the scores (stability).
> 2. **Equivalent/parallel forms**: give two comparable forms; correlate (equivalence).
> 3. **Split-half**: split one test (odd/even items), correlate the halves and correct with Spearman–Brown (internal consistency).
> 4. **Kuder–Richardson (KR-20/21) / Cronbach's alpha**: internal consistency from item statistics.
> 5. **Inter-rater**: two markers score the same scripts; correlate.
>
> **(b) Factors:**
> 1. **Test length**: longer tests are more reliable.
> 2. **Spread (variability) of scores**: wider spread → higher reliability.
> 3. **Item difficulty**: items too easy or too hard reduce reliability.
> 4. **Objectivity of scoring**: subjective marking lowers it.
> 5. **Testing conditions**: noise, poor lighting, cheating, fatigue.
> 6. **Time interval** (for test–retest) and **guessing**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reliability coefficients range from 0 to 1; classroom tests should aim for about 0.7 or higher.

## Simplified explanation

Test–retest, parallel forms, split-half, KR/alpha, inter-rater; length, spread, difficulty, scoring, conditions.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: Differentiate between a **standardised achievement test** and a **classroom (teacher-made) achievement test** under: test developer; who determines the content; test manual; usefulness.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | | Standardised | Classroom |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Developer** | Test experts/agencies (e.g. WAEC) | The class teacher |
> | **Content** | Determined by experts from a broad, common curriculum | Determined by the teacher from what was taught |
> | **Manual** | Has a manual with directions, norms, reliability/validity data | Usually none |
> | **Usefulness** | Comparing learners across schools/regions; selection, placement | Diagnosing and grading learners in that class; guiding instruction |
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Standardised tests have uniform administration and scoring and are norm-referenced; classroom tests are flexible and tied to local instruction.

## Simplified explanation

Experts vs teacher; broad vs local content; manual vs none; comparison vs class decisions.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: Describe **five** guidelines to consider when **assembling** test items after they have been constructed.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. **Group items by type** (all MCQs together, then short answer, then essay) so instructions apply to each section.
> 2. **Arrange from easy to difficult** to build confidence.
> 3. **Write clear general and section instructions** (time, marks, how to answer).
> 4. **Avoid patterns in the answer key**; spread correct options randomly across A–D.
> 5. **Keep each item, with its options, on one page**; don't split stems from options.
> 6. **Space items clearly and number them consecutively**; provide answer spaces.
> 7. **Ensure no item gives a clue** to another, and proofread before printing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Good assembly reduces construct-irrelevant difficulty and errors.

## Simplified explanation

Group by type, easy → hard, clear instructions, random key, keep items together.
hint: Give the points with a brief explanation each.

body: (a) 'There was a test after a long vacation.' Discuss **two** consequences of this for the test taker. (b) Discuss **four** pieces of information you would give students to prepare them for maximum performance. (c) Explain **two** ways to minimise test anxiety in the examination hall.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(a)** Learners may have **forgotten** much of what was taught, so scores **underestimate** their ability (low validity); unannounced testing raises **anxiety** and lowers motivation.
>
> **(b)** Tell students: (1) **when** the test will be; (2) **content/topics** covered; (3) **type and number of items** (MCQ, essay); (4) **time allowed and marks**; (5) how it will be **scored** and the materials needed.
>
> **(c)** Give **clear, calm instructions** and a reassuring atmosphere; begin with **easy items**; avoid threats or announcing that the test is 'very hard'; allow adequate time; ensure a comfortable, quiet room.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Test preparation and good administration improve the validity of results.

## Simplified explanation

Forgetting and anxiety; tell them when, what, format, time, scoring; calm environment.
